title: O3 – Structure: organisation charts and Mintzberg
source: Zusammenfassung von Session 3 „Structure“ und der Übersicht OM_Session3_Summary

blocks.text: The organisational dilemma: work must be divided (differentiation) and then coordinated (integration). Structure is the way to group employees into units while ensuring sufficient coordination to achieve efficiency.
The organisation chart shows only the grouping (functional, divisional, matrix). Mintzberg's “bottom perspective” shows how work is actually coordinated and who holds power.
Mintzberg: 5 coordination mechanisms, 5 parts of the organisation and 5 configurations. An organisation uses all mechanisms, but one is usually dominant.
To identify a configuration in a case, ask: how is work mostly coordinated? Who holds the power? Does the situation (age, size, environment, technology) fit?

Activities grouped by work function, each with its own hierarchy; top management coordinates. + Economies of scale, transparency, tight control. − Conflicts between functions, slow adaptation, overloaded top when the firm grows.

Divisions by product, customer type or region, each with its own functions and run as a profit centre; HQ or results coordinate. + Suits very large firms, accountability, responsiveness to customers. − Duplication, high coordination cost, competition between divisions.

Two logics overlaid (functions × projects, regions or customers). + Flexibility to take on projects and move resources, advantages of both. − Conflicts from a dual line of authority, hard to implement (example: Unilever segments × functions).
One person is responsible for the work of others and gives orders (hierarchy).
The content of the work is specified in rules or routines; coordination happens before the activity.
Expected results are made clear; the way to reach them is not prescribed.
Standardised training and education: people know what to expect of each other and coordinate almost automatically.
Informal communication between people doing interdependent work.
Class exercise: bar with a fixed process → work processes · traders must gain +15 % whatever the method → outputs · basketball players → mutual adjustment · Roman wars → direct supervision.
Top management; ensures the organisation is efficient and serves those who control it (CEO, board).
Managers connecting the apex with the operating core (division director, director of production, foreman).
Performs the basic work of producing products and services (machine operators, sales force, nurses).
Analysts who design, plan, change or train the operating core's work (planning, methods, training, quality).
Support outside the operating flow (cleaning, legal, cafeteria, PR).

Direct supervision · strategic apex · pull to centralise. Young/small firm, simple environment; or any firm in crisis. + speed, flexibility, low cost. − overloaded, charismatic leader; inadequate when size grows. Start-ups, architect office, special army operation.

Standardisation of work processes · technostructure · pull to standardise. Big, mature, simple and stable environment, routine mass technology. + efficiency, economies of scale, rules replace discretion. − vertical communication only, obsession with rules, slow adaptation, well-being of the operating core. Heavy industry, public administration.

Standardisation of outputs · middle line · pull to balkanise. Big, mature firm in diversified markets. + accountability, spreads risks, units can be removed. − duplication, divisional conflicts, excessive focus on outcomes. > 60 % of the Fortune 500; General Motors (Sloan).

Standardisation of skills · operating core · pull to professionalise. Complex but stable environment, external qualification standards. + expertise, autonomy, self-control by professionals. − coordination between professionals, conflicts with support staff, rejection of innovation. Hospitals, universities, big consulting firms.

Mutual adjustment · support staff (experts) · pull to collaborate. Complex, dynamic environment where innovation is critical. + the only truly innovative configuration, flexible. − costly coordination, tension, ambiguity → pull back toward bureaucracy. Research labs, small consulting firms, task forces, early NASA.
Structure ≠ organisation chart: structure = grouping plus coordination.
Divisional form: the key part is the middle line, the mechanism is standardisation of outputs (not processes).
Technostructure shapes the core's work (planning, methods, training); support staff serves outside the work flow (cleaning, legal).
Adhocracy is not “no coordination”: it coordinates by mutual adjustment – and that is costly.
Machine vs professional bureaucracy: processes vs skills, technostructure vs operating core, centralised vs decentralised, simple vs complex environment – both need stability.
